title: Scalable Bayesian Inference for Nonlinear Conservation Laws
claim: Our probabilistic method recovers hidden source fields more accurately than a neural baseline and also quantifies its uncertainty.
layout: 2x4 heatmap grid with four method columns and two colorbars; sensor dots and source stars overlaid
description: Eight heatmap panels in a 2x4 grid, labeled (a)–(h), with columns titled Ground truth, PINN, GP-FVM (mean) and GP-FVM (std). The top row shows the concentration field, using a viridis colormap. The bottom row shows the inferred source field, using a black-red-yellow colormap. White dots mark sensor locations. Cyan or white stars mark the true source positions. The PINN source estimate is blurry and has artifacts, with RMSE 0.76. The GP-FVM mean is closer to the ground truth, with RMSE 0.44. The std panels use a purple-yellow colormap and show uncertainty that is low near the sensors and high away from them. Four colorbars sit at the right, for concentration, concentration std, source and source std. The eye goes first to the bright source blobs in the bottom row, then compares them across columns.
caption: Source identification from sparse sensor measurements. Top row: concentration field. Bottom row: inferred source field. Our GP-FVM method (right) recovers the source locations with quantified uncertainty, while a PINN baseline produces a point estimate with artifacts. Our method solves this nonparametric problem in seconds; the PINN requires minutes.
abstract: Nonlinear conservation laws are at the heart of many of the most important dynamical systems in science and engineering. In practical applications, such systems are often subject to various sources of uncertainty, e.g. due to sparse or noisy measurements. Inferring physical quantities and fields of interest then becomes an ill-posed problem which both classical numerical methods and modern deep learning-based methods struggle to treat appropriately. Recent work has framed classical numerical methods as Bayesian inference under Gaussian process priors, resulting in a physics-aware treatment of uncertainties. Following this line of work, we develop a novel numerically conservative method for uncertainty-aware simulations of nonlinear conservation laws. We use recent sparse approximation techniques to scale up to large-scale forward and inverse problems. For forward simulation, we inherit the accuracy of classical solvers while providing structured uncertainty quantification. On inverse problems, we recover posteriors over nonparametric source fields in seconds -- outperforming neural baselines that take minutes to produce a less accurate point estimate.
